title: Piano Concerto in A minor
hook: A drum roll, a crash down the keyboard, and Norway arrives in the concert hall.

painting.title: Bridal Procession on the Hardangerfjord
painting.pairingNote: Norway’s best-loved picture of its own fjords and folk life, painted twenty years before the concerto; the same national romance that Grieg’s dances carry into the concert hall.

facts: Grieg wrote the concerto in the summer of 1868 in Søllerød, near Copenhagen, where he had gone for the country air. He was 24. It is the only concerto he completed.
He knew Schumann’s Piano Concerto well, having heard Clara Schumann play it in Leipzig as a student. He chose the same key, A minor, and a similar opening flourish.

The first performance was in Copenhagen on 3 April 1869, with Edmund Neupert as soloist. In 1870 Liszt sight-read it from the manuscript in Rome and praised it. Grieg kept revising the concerto for the rest of his life, until a few weeks before his death.

It sounds Norwegian from the first bar: the falling opening figure is typical of Norwegian folk song, and the finale is a halling, a leaping folk dance, with echoes of the Hardanger fiddle. In 1909 it became the first piano concerto ever recorded, in a version cut to six minutes.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dramatic crash and a song (I), a hushed nocturne for muted strings (II), a stamping folk dance that ends in a hymn (III).

movements.heading: Allegro molto moderato
movements.summary: One of the most famous openings in music: a drum roll, then the piano crashes down the whole keyboard. What follows is gentler than that start suggests, a movement of songs more than battles, in [[sonata-form|sonata form]]. Near the end the piano has a long [[cadenza|cadenza]] that grows from a whisper to a roar.

mainIdeas.name: The flourish
mainIdeas.description: a falling figure that crashes down the keyboard in loud chords and octaves.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, slightly march-like tune, first in the woodwinds, then in the piano.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a warm, singing melody in C major, first on the cellos.

stops.hear: A drum roll swells; the piano crashes down from the top of the keyboard to the bottom in loud chords
stops.happening: The famous opening. The falling figure is the seed of the whole movement

stops.hear: Flutes, oboes and clarinets, softly, play a gentle, slightly marching tune
The piano takes the tune and decorates it
Livelier: skipping rhythms pass between piano and orchestra
The music settles; the cellos sing a broad, warm melody
The piano takes up the melody and makes it grander
stops.happening: Theme 2 on the piano. The end of the [[exposition|exposition]] approaches

stops.hear: Quieter and more searching: the opening tune drifts through the orchestra while the piano ripples around it
The marching tune returns in A minor
The warm melody comes back, now in A major
stops.happening: Theme 2 in the home key, brightened

stops.hear: The orchestra stops. The piano alone starts quietly, then builds to thundering chords over rumbling bass [[tremolo|tremolo]]s

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The orchestra returns, faster; the movement ends with the same crash down the keyboard as at the start
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]]. The opening flourish closes the movement

notice: The opening crash returns at the very end. Listen for it in the last seconds of the movement.
Liszt suggested giving Theme 2 to a trumpet instead of the cellos. Grieg tried it, then changed it back.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: A slow, hushed song in D-flat major, far from the A minor of the first movement. The [[muted|muted]] strings play a long, calm melody; the piano answers with its own decorated, dreamy music, and later takes the melody itself, in full, ringing chords. The end leads straight into the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The string melody
mainIdeas.description: long, slow and quiet, on muted violins, rising and falling gently.

mainIdeas.name: The piano’s song
mainIdeas.description: delicate, decorated phrases, with quick little groups of five and six notes.

stops.hear: Very soft, veiled strings play a long, calm melody
stops.happening: The main melody, on muted strings

stops.hear: The orchestra falls quiet; the piano enters with soft, ornamented phrases high up
stops.happening: The piano’s own music, a dreamy answer

stops.hear: The piano grows warmer and more urgent; the orchestra joins in
The piano plays the string melody itself, loud, in full chords; the whole orchestra supports it
stops.happening: The climax. The melody has passed from the strings to the piano

stops.hear: Calm again; the piano’s phrases float upward over soft strings

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: A soft hold, and then the finale begins without a break

notice: Compare the melody at the start, on muted strings, with the piano’s version at ≈ 4:15. Same tune, opposite colour.

movements.heading: Allegro moderato molto e marcato – Quasi presto – Andante maestoso
movements.tempo: Allegro moderato molto e marcato – Quasi presto – Andante maestoso
movements.summary: A Norwegian dance finale. The piano stamps out a halling, a leaping folk dance, against sharp chords in the orchestra. In the middle a solo flute plays a calm, high melody, like a hymn to nature. At the end that hymn returns in full glory, and the concerto finishes in A major.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: an accented tune in 2/4, with piano and orchestra trading the strong and weak beats. It is modelled on the halling.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: a calm, wide melody in F major, first on a solo flute in its highest register.

stops.hear: Quiet, pointed chords in the clarinets and bassoons; the piano answers with a quick run
The piano stamps out a lively dance with strong accents; the orchestra answers on the off-beats
stops.happening: Theme 1, the halling, in A minor

stops.hear: Orchestra and piano toss the dance back and forth; it grows louder
stops.happening: The dance develops, at times in full [[tutti|tutti]]

stops.hear: Everything stops dancing. A solo flute, very high and quiet, plays a calm melody over soft strings
stops.happening: Theme 2, the hymn, in F major

stops.hear: The piano takes up the melody, gently
The dance returns and is thrown between piano and orchestra again
A short flourish on the piano alone
The dance turns into a fast, whirling three-beat dance, now in A major
The whole orchestra plays the flute’s hymn at full strength, in A major; the piano crashes out huge chords
stops.happening: *Andante maestoso*: the hymn becomes the finale’s climax

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A last rush and the closing chords

notice: In the dance, listen to who plays on the strong beats. The piano and the orchestra take turns, like two dancers stamping.
The flute’s quiet hymn at ≈ 2:30 is the same melody that ends the concerto in full orchestra.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Zimerman recorded the concerto with Karajan and the Berliner Philharmoniker in the Philharmonie in September 1981, in digital sound, then still new. On the Spotify album the Grieg is tracks 4–6, after Schumann’s concerto.

threads.title: Norway in the concert hall
threads.body: Folk-song shapes in the first movement, a halling in the last. Grieg was 24 and wanted his music to sound like home.

threads.title: Song before battle
threads.body: The piano spends as much time singing and accompanying as it does showing off.

threads.title: From A minor to A major
threads.body: The concerto starts with a dark crash and ends with a hymn in the major.
